figures.caption: Figure 1: Motivation and overview of FoRM. Left: Static KD forces the student to directly match the teacher without intermediate guidance, leaving the optimisation path undefined.Middle: FoRM constructs structured flow-map anchors z1, z2, z3 along the distillation trajectory. Right: Relation map comparison onUrban100. FoRMachieves significantly higher top-6 patch overlap (71% vs. 33%) and CKA (0.9847 vs. 0.8153) with the teacher, indicating better relational structure alignment.

Figure 2: Overview of the FoRM framework. Teacher and student features are extracted at layers ℓ ∈ {2, 5, 8}, pooled to 8×8, and converted to softmax-normalised relation matrices 𝑅𝑡 and 𝑅𝑠 via a shared Relation Head. Ground-truth bridge states 𝑧𝑡 , 𝑧𝑠 are constructed by linear interpolation between student and teacher relation states; the flow map head F𝜃 predicts relation states at arbitrary target times. Three losses, Lmap, Lbd, and Lsg, jointly supervise F𝜃 under schedule weight𝑤 (𝜌). state error accumulation [4, 30], a risk amplified in KD where both endpoints carry fixed semantic content. In the restoration domain, generative methods such as FlowSR [38], CTMSR [41], and FluxSR [18] have demonstrated flow-based trajectory modelling for one-step SR, as does ultra-high-resolution synthesis [36, 37]; all operate in the generative sampling regime and do not address discriminative restoration KD. FoRM fills this gap by learning F𝜃 on the relation manifold with a safe semigroup constraint conditioned on ground-truth bridge points, paired with endpoint anchoring to prevent manifold drift.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on four image restoration tasks. For deraining (img_53 in Rain100L), denoising (102061 in BSD68), and deblurring (000023 in GoPro), we adopt Restormer [43] as the teacher–student backbone. For super-resolution (×4) (img_066 in Urban100), we adopt RCAN [46]. Compared methods include FAKD [10], CSD [34], MTKD [14], DUKD [47], MiPKD [19], and DCKD [48]. FoRM (Ours) consistently recovers finer structural details with fewer artifacts across all four tasks.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on composite image degradation (CDD-11 [8] dataset), using Restormer [43] as the backbone. Each column corresponds to a different degradation combination: Low Light + Haze + Snow, Haze + Rain, Haze + Snow, Low Light + Haze + Rain, Low Light + Haze, and Low Light + Snow. From top to bottom: degraded input, DCKD [48], and FoRM (Ours). FoRM recovers cleaner textures and more faithful colors across all degradation combinations.

Table 1: Quantitative comparison of knowledge distillation methods for five-degradation all-in-one image restoration, using Restormer [43] as the teacher–student backbone. Results are reported as PSNR (dB)↑ / SSIM↑. Denoising is evaluated at noise level 𝜎 = 25. The Teacher row denotes the full Restormer upper bound; Scratch denotes student training without distillation.

Table 2: Quantitative comparison (×4 SR) of knowledge distillation methods across four backbone settings: SwinIR [20], RCAN [46], EDSR [21], and a cross-architecture setting. All results are reported as PSNR (dB) / SSIM on Set5, Set14, BSD100, and Urban100. The Teacher row denotes the full-model upper bound; Scratch denotes student training without distillation. The best and second-best results are bolded and underlined, respectively.

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on Urban100 (×4). For each example, we show the HR patch (ground truth), super-resolved patches from the Teacher, Static KD, and FoRM (Ours), along with their corresponding relation maps. FoRM achieves higher CKA with the Teacher’s relation map (0.9729 vs. 0.8803 on img_028; 0.9599 vs. 0.8948 on img_082), indicating better relational structure alignment, which correlates with improved PSNR and SSIM.
